cards.q: [Mar 2026 · Q1(a)] 1956: Astamor and Balala conclude the Investigation Convention (lead in the Xympora groundwater). 1982: Astamor, Balala and Cumo establish the international organisation XRHO by the Xympora Health Charter. 1984: Cumo ratifies the Lead Crisis Understanding with the XRHO. 1995: the three States conclude the LeadFree Pact with the company HydroClean to build purification plants. 1996: the three States conclude the Debt Allocation Agreement allocating the project debts among themselves. To which of these agreements is the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties applicable, and why or why not? (3 points)
cards.a:
VCLT applies only to the 1982 Charter and 1996 Agreement.
• Treaty between States (Art 1), written, governed by IL (Art 2(1)(a)), concluded after entry into force for them (27.1.1980, Art 4).
• 1956 Convention: pre-1980, no retroactivity (Art 4) → custom.
• 1982 Charter: post-1980 IO constituent instrument → applies (Art 5).
• 1984 Understanding: State–IO → outside VCLT (Art 1, 3); 1986 Convention not in force → custom.
• 1995 Pact: company not IL subject → no treaty (Anglo-Iranian Oil 1952).
• 1996 Agreement: inter-State, post-1980 → applies.

cards.q: [Mar 2026 · Q1(b)] Astamor and Balala concluded the 1956 Investigation Convention to investigate and combat the cause of rising lead levels in the Xympora groundwater. In 1994 researchers in Astamor developed a process that easily purifies groundwater of lead; in 1995 the States commissioned the company HydroClean to build twenty purification plants. Under what conditions does a State have the right to terminate a treaty? (5 points)
cards.a:
A State may terminate under the treaty, by consent, by an implied right or on a recognised ground, following the procedure.
• Termination clause (Art 54(a)); consent of all parties (Art 54(b); later treaty, Art 59).
• No clause: only if intended or implied by the treaty's nature, 12 months' notice (Art 56).
• Material breach by another party — repudiation or violation of an essential provision (Art 60); supervening impossibility — permanent loss of an indispensable object, not self-caused (Art 61).
• Fundamental change: essential basis of consent, unforeseen, radically transforms remaining obligations; not boundaries (Art 62; Gabčíkovo 1997); new ius cogens (Art 64); desuetude.
• Procedure: written notification, 3 months, dispute settlement (Art 65–67).
• Xympora: pre-1980 treaty → custom (Art 4); breakthrough is no impossibility, hardly a radical change → needs clause, consent, implied right or desuetude.

cards.q: [Mar 2026 · Q1(c)] Astamor, Balala and Cumo consider ending or pausing some of their lead agreements. How do the invalidity, termination and suspension of a treaty differ in their effects? (2 points)
cards.a:
Invalidity voids the treaty from the outset, termination ends it for the future, suspension only pauses it.
• Invalidity (Art 69): no legal force (ex tunc); restore the prior position; good-faith acts before invocation stay lawful.
• Termination (Art 70): no further performance (ex nunc); rights created before remain.
• Suspension (Art 72): performance paused, relations continue; no acts obstructing resumption.

cards.q: [Mar 2026 · Q2(a)] Is the ban on the use of force binding under international law? Can a powerful State threaten a weaker State with the use of force? Provide reasons for your answer. (3 points)
cards.a:
Yes, it binds all States; no — threats are equally prohibited, whatever a State's power.
• Art 2(4) UN Charter prohibits the threat or use of force → binds all members.
• Also custom (Nicaragua 1986, paras 188–190) → binds non-members; ius cogens (Art 53 VCLT); forced treaty void (Art 52 VCLT).
• Threat unlawful if the threatened force would be unlawful (Nuclear Weapons AO 1996, para 47); only Art 51 or Chapter VII force may be threatened.
• Power irrelevant: sovereign equality (Art 2(1)); SC may act (Art 39).

cards.q: [Mar 2026 · Q2(b)] What are the exceptions to the general prohibition of the use of force? (2 points)
cards.a:
Two exceptions: self-defence (Art 51) and Security Council measures under Chapter VII (Art 42).
• Art 51: armed attack, necessity, proportionality, report, until the SC acts.
• Art 39 determination → Art 42 or authorisation of 'all necessary means' (Res 678 (1990)).
• Government's invitation: not 'against' the State → no true exception.
• Contested: humanitarian intervention (Kosovo 1999), rescuing nationals, pre-emption; R2P no exception.

cards.q: [Mar 2026 · Q2(c)] Do you agree? Provide reasons. "When a State defends itself against the use of force, it may use any defensive measures at its disposal." (2 points)
cards.a:
No — self-defence is limited.
• Only against an armed attack (Art 51; Nicaragua 1986, para 191).
• Necessity and proportionality: only what repels the attack, no retaliation (Nicaragua para 176; Nuclear Weapons AO, para 41; Oil Platforms 2003).
• IHL binds the defender too (distinction, prohibited weapons).
• Report immediately to the SC; lasts only until the SC has taken necessary measures (Art 51).

cards.q: [Mar 2026 · Q3(a)] After cross-border cyberattacks on critical infrastructure in State Y, allegedly from State X, the Security Council adopts a Chapter VII resolution determining a threat to international peace and security and establishing an investigative mechanism to collect evidence of the cyber operations. The UN Charter does not explicitly mention investigative mechanisms. Can the Security Council lawfully establish such a mechanism? If so, on what legal basis? (3 points)
cards.a:
Yes — under Chapter VII after an Art 39 determination.
• Art 39: wide discretion; cyberattacks on critical infrastructure can be a threat to the peace.
• Art 41: non-military measures, list non-exhaustive ('may include') → ICTY/ICTR upheld (Tadić 1995); collecting evidence is a lesser measure.
• Art 29: subsidiary organs; Art 34: investigation of situations; practice: OPCW-UN JIM (2015), UNITAD (2017).
• Implied powers (Reparation 1949; Certain Expenses 1962); primary responsibility (Art 24(1)).
• Limits: purposes and principles (Art 24(2)); States must cooperate (Art 25).

cards.q: [Mar 2026 · Q3(b)] As the cyberattacks from State X on State Y continue, the Security Council votes on a second Chapter VII resolution imposing binding economic sanctions on X: 11 in favour, 1 against (a permanent member), 3 abstentions. Are UN member States obliged to implement these economic sanctions on State X? (3 points)
cards.a:
No — the permanent member's 'no' is a veto, so no resolution was adopted.
• Art 27(3): non-procedural → 9 affirmative votes including the concurring votes of the permanent members; 11 yes suffice, but one P5 'no' defeats it; abstentions are no veto (Namibia AO 1971); no duty to abstain under Chapter VII.
• No decision → no obligation under Art 25.
• GA cannot replace it — only recommends (Res 377(V)).
• States may still adopt autonomous sanctions: retorsion, or countermeasures by an injured State (ARSIWA Arts 49–54).

cards.q: [Jan 2026 · Q2(a)] Explain the different forms of state succession and give examples. (5 points)
cards.a:
Forms differ by whether the predecessor survives and a new state emerges; a mere change of government is no succession.
• Dismembratio (dissolution): predecessor disappears, several new states (Austria-Hungary 1918, SFRY 1991–92, Czechoslovakia 1993).
• Secession (against the parent's will) / separation (by agreement): a part becomes a new state, predecessor continues (Bangladesh 1971, Eritrea 1993, South Sudan 2011; USSR 1991, Russia continuing).
• Merger/fusion: states unite into a new one, all predecessors disappear (Tanzania 1964, Yemen 1990).
• Incorporation (absorption): one state absorbs another and continues (GDR into FRG 1990); only lawful succession counts (Art 6 VCST) → forcible annexation ≠ succession (Austria 1938, Kuwait 1990, Crimea 2014).
• Cession/transfer of territory between existing states (Alaska 1867, Hong Kong 1997) → moving treaty frontiers (Art 15 VCST).
• Newly independent states from decolonisation (Art 2(1)(f) VCST; Algeria 1962).

cards.q: [Jan 2026 · Q2(b)] Name the sources of law applicable to state succession in respect of treaties and outline the different principles in that respect. (5 points)
cards.a:
Sources: VCST 1978, custom and case-specific agreements/declarations; principles: moving frontiers, clean slate, continuity — territorial treaties always pass.
• VCST 1978 (in force 1996, few parties, only later successions, Art 7) + custom (decisive) + devolution agreements (not binding on third states, Art 8) and unilateral declarations (Art 9).
• Theories: universal succession, tabula rasa, pick and choose.
• Moving treaty frontiers (Art 15): transferred territory leaves the predecessor's treaties, enters the acquirer's.
• Clean slate for newly independent states (Art 16); multilateral treaties by notification of succession (Art 17), bilateral only by agreement (Art 24).
• Continuity: uniting of states (Art 31), separation and dissolution (Art 34, unless agreed or incompatible); continuing state keeps its treaties (Art 35).
• Always: boundaries and territorial regimes survive (Arts 11–12; Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros 1997); political treaties (alliances) lapse.

Lirania has mined it since 2022; Monturia initially protested, then took no further action, and sued before the ICJ in 2025. Lirania argues Monturia forfeited its right by long silence. Monturia demands compensation for the minerals extracted plus default interest; Lirania says the claims are time-barred and no treaty provides for interest. cards.a:
General principles of law (Art 38(1)(c) ICJ Statute) are unwritten principles common to the main national legal systems or formed within international law that fill gaps; the three relevant ones favour Monturia.
• Two categories: from national systems (transposable) and formed within IL; gap filling → no non liquet.
• (1) Acquiescence/estoppel (good faith): silence = consent only where a reaction was called for (Temple 1962) → Monturia protested and sued within 3 years → no forfeiture.
• (2) Extinctive prescription: no fixed time limit; only unreasonable delay prejudicing the respondent bars a claim (Nauru 1992) → not time-barred.
• (3) Full reparation (Chorzów Factory 1928; Art 31 ARSIWA): if the valley is Monturian → compensation for the minerals (Art 36) plus interest (Art 38) → no treaty basis needed.
• Other examples: res judicata, nemo iudex in causa sua.

• Breach of due diligence/no-harm (Trail Smelter) = responsibility.

• Art 7: ultra vires acts in official capacity are still attributed (Caire 1929).
• Art 8: private persons acting on the State's instructions or under its direction or effective control (Nicaragua 1986; Bosnian Genocide 2007, not Tadić's overall control).
• Art 9: governmental authority exercised in the absence or default of the authorities (Yeager 1987); Art 10: successful insurrectional movement (new government or new State).
• Art 11: conduct acknowledged and adopted as its own (Tehran Hostages 1980).

cards.q: [May 2025 · Q3] After a change of government, the new President of State X wants to withdraw from all bilateral and multilateral treaties protecting the environment, the climate and biodiversity, if possible in accordance with international law. Give 5 proposals her cabinet could submit, assess their prospects of success and distinguish which are relatively easy, which difficult and which have little chance of success. (10 points)
cards.a:
Easy: the treaties' own withdrawal clauses; difficult: consent of all parties or Art 56 VCLT; little chance: material breach or fundamental change of circumstances.
• 1 EASY — withdrawal under the treaty's clause (Art 54(a) VCLT): e.g. Paris Agreement Art 28 (notice any time after 3 years in force for X, effective 1 year after receipt; USA); bilateral treaties: termination with notice; instrument signed by Head of State/Government or Foreign Minister (Art 67(2) VCLT).
• 2 DIFFICULT — termination by consent of all parties (Art 54(b) VCLT) or by a later treaty (Art 59 VCLT): bilateral negotiable, multilateral (~200 parties) practically hopeless.
• 3 DIFFICULT — treaty without withdrawal clause (Art 56 VCLT): only if the parties intended it or the nature of the treaty implies it, 12 months' notice → doubtful for common-interest environmental treaties.
• 4 LITTLE CHANCE — material breach by another party (Art 60 VCLT): essential provision violated by a specific party, multilateral only under Art 60(2); no pretext (Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros 1997).
• 5 LITTLE CHANCE — fundamental change of circumstances (Art 62 VCLT): new policy or costs are no radical change of an essential basis (Fisheries Jurisdiction 1973; Gabčíkovo 1997); likewise impossibility (Art 61), desuetude (treaties are applied), invalidity (Arts 46–53, acquiescence Art 45) and re-accession with reservations (banned: Paris Art 27, UNFCCC Art 24, CBD Art 37 → Art 19(a) VCLT).
• Limits: change of government is no excuse (Arts 26–27 VCLT); procedure Arts 65–67 VCLT; simply stopping performance = wrongful act → state responsibility; customary no-harm/EIA duties remain (Art 43 VCLT; Pulp Mills 2010).

cards.q: [Jun 2024 · Q1(a)] Bellivonia is being divided by agreement into Bellistan (over 80% of the territory) and Livonia. Bellistan claims to continue Bellivonia's legal identity under a new name as the 'rump state', with only Livonia a new state; Livonia says Bellivonia has ceased to exist and both are successor states. What does 'state succession' mean? (2 points)
cards.a:
State succession = replacement of one state by another in the responsibility for the international relations of a territory (Art 2(1)(b) VCST 1978; Art 2(1)(a) VCSSPAD 1983).
• Change of sovereignty, not of government or name → identity continues.
• Question: which treaties, property, debts pass; only lawful successions (Art 6 VCST).
• A continuing state (Bellistan's claim) is no successor → only Livonia.

Bellistan claims to be Bellivonia under a new name (rump state), with only Livonia new; Livonia says Bellivonia has ceased to exist and both are successor states. How is the division classified on Bellistan's view? What type of state succession does Livonia's view represent? Briefly justify. (4 points)
cards.a:
Bellistan's view = continuity of Bellivonia (rump state) plus separation of Livonia; Livonia's view = dismembratio (dissolution) into two successor states.
• Bellistan: predecessor survives with less territory; name change and territorial loss do not affect identity → only Livonia is new (Russia/USSR 1991, Sudan 2011).
• Consequences: Bellistan keeps treaties (Art 35 VCST) and UN seat; Livonia succeeds (Art 34 VCST), applies to the UN; property and debts shared (Arts 17, 40 VCSSPAD).
• Livonia: predecessor extinct, two equal new states (Czechoslovakia 1993; SFRY, Badinter Opinions 8, 10).
• Consequences: both apply to the UN; treaties continue for each (Art 34 VCST); property, archives, debts divided equitably (Arts 18, 31, 41 VCSSPAD).

cards.q: [Jun 2024 · Q2(a)] A, B and C, humanitarian associations from three different countries, discuss founding an international organization. A's Secretary General doubts this, since only states can found international organizations and A, B and C are associations. Can an international organization only be founded by states, or also by other legal entities? (2 points)
cards.a:
Partly right: besides states, IOs can found IOs, but private associations like A, B and C cannot.
• IO = established by treaty or other instrument governed by IL (Art 2(a) ARIO) → founders need treaty-making capacity: states, IOs.
• EC founding WTO member 1995; EEC and EIB founded EBRD 1990.
• Associations lack treaty capacity → private-law contract → international NGO, not IO.

cards.q: [Jun 2024 · Q2(b)] A, B and C, humanitarian associations, discuss founding an international organization. A's Secretary General says only states can found one. B's president disagrees, citing the Red Cross as a model. Is the 'Red Cross' an international organization? To what extent could it serve as a model for A, B and C? (4 points)
cards.a:
No: the ICRC is a private association under Swiss law with partial (functional) international personality conferred by states → only a limited model.
• Not an IO: association under Art 60 Swiss Civil Code, not founded by treaty, no state members (likewise Federation, national societies).
• Partial personality: mandate in Geneva Conventions 1949/APs 1977 (POW visits, tracing, humanitarian initiative, common Art 3); HQ agreement with Switzerland 1993; GA observer 1990; ICTY Simić 1999.
• Limit: non-state personality depends on conferral by states → cannot be self-created; ICRC rests on 150 years' practice.
• Options: NGOs with ECOSOC consultative status (Art 71 UN Charter), host-state agreements, or states found a real IO by treaty.

cards.q: [Jun 2024 · Q3(a)] Rachastan and Antrania have disputed the region of Bethania since independence 45 years ago; the colonial power assigned it to Antrania although over 90% of its inhabitants are ethnic Rachastanis. They have fought three wars, and after the assassination of an Antranian politician in Bethania a new war threatens. The St. Petersburg Federation, a third state, wants to help them reach a peaceful settlement. What options do third parties (non-disputing states) have to support the parties in reaching an agreement? Explain the procedures and the role of the third party in each. (8 points)
cards.a:
Third parties can offer the non-binding diplomatic means of Art 33(1) UN Charter (good offices, inquiry, mediation, conciliation) with rising involvement, each only with the consent of both parties.
• Framework: duty of peaceful settlement (Art 2(3) UN Charter); Art 33(1) = menu, free choice of means (consensualism); negotiation itself has no third party.
• Good offices: no influence on content; third party provides venue, communication channels, logistics so the parties talk without losing face (Iran deal, Vienna 2015; UN SG) → St. Petersburg hosts talks.
• Inquiry: commission (parity, agreed rules) establishes disputed facts in a non-binding report, no legal conclusions (Hague Conventions 1899/1907; Dogger Bank 1904) → clarify the assassination.
• Mediation: third party actively proposes non-binding terms, may exert influence, offer incentives, work confidentially (Algeria, Iran–US 1980–81) → e.g. autonomy, minority guarantees or referendum for Bethania.
• Conciliation: formalised inquiry + mediation; commission examines facts and law, hears the parties, proposes a non-binding compromise (Jan Mayen 1981; Timor-Leste/Australia 2016–18).
• UN: SC may investigate (Art 34), recommend procedures or terms (Arts 36–37, Chapter VI); regional agencies (Art 52). Contrast: arbitration/ICJ bind, also only with consent.

cards.q: [Apr 2024 · Q1(a)] (April 2024 exam) State Willunia has dissolved; its successor State Selenur announces that its courts will hear claims against foreign states even for acts performed in the exercise of sovereign authority. The President of Cornistan replies: "Sovereign immunity is part of customary international law. It is based on a strong sense of legal obligation of the community of states." What does "sense of legal obligation" mean? How can a state express it? What is the second constitutive element of customary international law? (3 points)
cards.a:
It means opinio iuris (practice accepted as law); the second element is general state practice.
• Art 38(1)(b) ICJ Statute: custom = "general practice accepted as law"; both elements needed (ILC 2018 Concl. 2).
• Opinio iuris = acting from a sense of legal obligation, not courtesy (North Sea 1969).
• Expressed by (Concl. 10): public statements, diplomatic notes (like Cornistan's), legal opinions, court decisions, treaties, IO resolution votes; silence where reaction called for.
• Practice (Concl. 6, 8): physical and verbal acts (legislation, court decisions); widespread, representative, consistent.

cards.q: [Apr 2024 · Q1(b)] (April 2024 exam) Selenur, a new state that emerged from the dissolution of Willunia, refuses to grant foreign states immunity for sovereign acts, arguing: "Since the founding of our state our government has criticised sovereign immunity. Therefore Selenur is a persistent objector and not bound by it." What can a persistent objector achieve with its protest? What must a state do to be a persistent objector? Can Selenur be a persistent objector? (4 points)
cards.a:
No — Selenur objects too late: immunity was settled custom before Selenur existed.
• Effect: the rule binds all others, but is not opposable to the objector while it maintains its objection (ILC 2018 Concl. 15(1); Anglo-Norwegian Fisheries 1951).
• Conditions (Concl. 15(1)–(2)): objection while the rule is forming, clearly expressed, made known to other states, maintained persistently; impossible against ius cogens (ILC 2022 Concl. 14(3)).
• Application: immunity is long-established custom (Germany v Italy 2012); a new state is bound by custom in force at its birth; no Willunia objection to continue → at most a subsequent objector.
• → Selenur is bound; denying immunity for acta iure imperii is an internationally wrongful act.

cards.q: [Apr 2024 · Q1(c)] (April 2024 exam) Selenur argues: "Sovereign immunity cannot be customary law, because not all states were actively involved in creating it. The consent of states is the pillar of the international legal order, so all states must participate in creating a rule of customary law." Do all states have to participate in creating a norm of customary international law? What else does the requirement of "generality of practice" mean? (3 points)
cards.a:
No — practice must be general, not universal; non-participating states are bound unless they are persistent objectors.
• Widespread and representative (regions, legal systems), including specially affected states (ILC 2018 Concl. 8(1); North Sea 1969: "extensive and virtually uniform").
• Consistent: "constant and uniform usage" (Asylum 1950); deviations treated as breaches do not prevent the rule (Nicaragua 1986).
• No minimum duration (Concl. 8(2)).
• Consent is tacit: silence while the rule forms = acquiescence; new states are bound by existing custom → immunity binds Selenur.

cards.q: [Apr 2024 · Q2(a)] (April 2024 exam) In 2023 the Foreign Minister of State A signed the UNESCO 'Convention for the Protection of Ancient Monuments' (subject to ratification), which prohibits demolition and significant constructional changes of protected buildings. What further steps, internationally and domestically, are required after the signature for the Convention to bind and be applied in State A? (4 points)
cards.a:
Signature subject to ratification does not yet bind (Art 14 VCLT); these steps follow.
• Domestic approval by parliament (Austria: Art 50(1) Z 1 B-VG).
• Ratification = international consent (Arts 2(1)(b), 14 VCLT) by the Head of State, no full powers needed (Art 7(2)(a); Austria: Art 65(1) B-VG).
• Deposit with the UNESCO Director-General → consent established (Art 16(b)).
• Entry into force per treaty terms, for a later ratifier on its own date (Art 24(1), (3)) → bound (Art 26).
• UN registration (Art 102 Charter, Art 80 VCLT; no validity condition); domestic publication, implementing laws if not self-executing (Art 50(2) Z 4 B-VG).
• Meanwhile Art 18: no defeating object and purpose.

Furthermore, a state is allowed to defend itself against terrorists. What are the exceptions to the ban on the use of force? Explain them briefly. • GA: wrong — self-defence is an inherent right needing no permission; GA only recommends (Arts 10–14, 11(2); Certain Expenses 1962), even under Uniting for Peace (Res 377(V)).
• Terrorists: lawful if the attack is attributable to a state (Nicaragua para 195) or with the territorial state's consent; against non-state actors as such contested: ICJ requires a state attack (Wall 2004, para 139), but Res 1368/1373 (2001) and "unable or unwilling" practice support it → Rachel partly right.

cards.q: [Mar 2024 · Q1(a)] Name the different models of state succession. Provide examples. (3 points)
cards.a:
Four models — dissolution, secession/separation, merger, incorporation — plus cession and decolonisation.
• Succession = one state replaces another in responsibility for a territory's international relations (Art 2(1)(b) VCST).
• Dissolution (dismembratio): predecessor disappears, e.g. SFRY 1991–92, Czechoslovakia 1993.
• Secession/separation: predecessor continues, e.g. Montenegro 2006, South Sudan 2011, USSR 1991 (Russia continues).
• Merger: new state replaces all, e.g. Tanzania 1964, Yemen 1990.
• Incorporation: absorption, e.g. GDR into FRG 1990; forcible annexation ≠ succession (Art 6 VCST).
• Cession: Alaska 1867, Hong Kong 1997; decolonisation: Algeria 1962.

cards.q: [Mar 2024 · Q1(b)] What are the consequences of the different models of state succession for succession in treaties? From which legal sources do the rules of state succession derive? (5 points)
cards.a:
Consequences depend on model and treaty type; sources: 1978 and 1983 Vienna Conventions, custom, agreements.
• Theories: automatic succession, clean slate (tabula rasa), pick and choose.
• Separation: predecessor keeps its treaties (Art 35 VCST); each successor, also after dissolution, stays bound by treaties in force for its territory unless agreed otherwise or incompatible (Art 34) → Czech Republic, Slovakia 1993.
• Merger: treaties continue only for their old territory (Art 31); incorporation in practice = moving frontiers (Germany 1990).
• Cession: moving treaty frontiers (Art 15); newly independent states: clean slate (Art 16), may join multilateral treaties by notification (Art 17).
• Always pass: boundaries, territorial regimes (Arts 11–12; Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros 1997); alliances never.
• Sources: VCST 1978 (in force 1996, not retroactive, Art 7); 1983 Convention on property, archives, debts (not in force); custom (decisive); devolution agreements, declarations.

cards.q: [Mar 2024 · Q3] Ken and Barbie are debating United Nations peacekeeping operations. Ken claims that such operations are established by the General Assembly in accordance with the UN Charter and serve strictly military purposes. Barbie disagrees: in her view peacekeeping operations may be used only in inter-state conflicts, since otherwise they would be incompatible with the UN Charter. Explain the concept of peacekeeping operations, especially their legal basis and scope of functions, and address the arguments of Ken and Barbie. (10 points)
cards.a:
Both are wrong: peacekeeping operations are created mainly by the Security Council on implied powers, are multidimensional and are often deployed in internal conflicts.
• Concept: UN military, police and civilian personnel ('blue helmets') contributed voluntarily by members to help create and keep conditions for lasting peace; neither Chapter VI nor Art 42 → 'Chapter VI½'.
• Legal basis: no express Charter provision; implied powers serving Art 1(1) (Certain Expenses 1962) → costs are expenses of the Organization (Art 17(2)); plus Arts 24, 29, 40, a maiore ad minus from Chapter VII, and accepted practice.
• Principles: consent of the host state and parties, impartiality, force only in self-defence and defence of the mandate; subsidiary organ under SC authority, directed by the Secretary-General.
• Functions: classical – monitoring ceasefires and buffer zones (UNFICYP, UNDOF); multidimensional since 1989 – disarmament, police, elections, human rights, transitional administration (UNTAC, UNMIK); robust Chapter VII mandates to protect civilians (MONUSCO Intervention Brigade, Res 2098 (2013)).
• Ken wrong: the SC establishes virtually all operations (primary responsibility, Art 24); the GA only exceptionally and consent-based – UNEF I 1956 under Uniting for Peace, since Art 11(2) 'action' means enforcement only (Certain Expenses); 'in accordance with the Charter' only via implied powers; not strictly military – police and civilian components, and even classical missions monitored rather than fought.
• Barbie wrong: ONUC (Congo 1960), MONUSCO and UNMISS operate in internal conflicts. Compatible with the Charter: host consent → no intervention; internal conflicts may threaten international peace (Art 39; Tadić 1995); Art 2(7) does not bar Chapter VII measures.

After a change of government, A's new digitalization minister calls the treaty a restriction of free competition, and A declares to the other States that it will not ratify. The treaty enters into force among the other States on 1 July 2024. Is State A bound by the treaty? (2 points)

cards.q: [Feb 2024 · Q2(a)] Stardust, a company based in State Y, operates thousands of small satellites in Earth orbit providing cheap internet access (1,000 launched in 2021, 1,500 in 2022). • Rapid custom: Sputnik 1957 overflights unprotested → opinio iuris by acquiescence (ILC Concl. 10(3)); short duration suffices (North Sea 1969).

• Custom binds X outside the OST; protesting only now → no persistent objector → claim fails.

cards.q: [Feb 2024 · Q3(b)] The president of Cumri adds that even if Cumri were a party to the ICCPR, it would only be obliged to refrain from interfering with individual rights, with no requirement to take positive action to protect human rights. What are states' obligations under international human rights law with regard to individual human rights? (3 points)
cards.a:
The president is wrong: human rights oblige states to respect, protect and fulfil.
• Respect: negative duty — state organs must not interfere (no torture, arbitrary arrest, censorship).
• Protect: positive duty against private interference — prevent, investigate, punish, redress (due diligence), e.g. police protecting demonstrators.
• Fulfil: create legal, institutional and material conditions — courts, legal aid, elections, humane prisons.
• Basis: Art 2(1) ICCPR "respect and ensure" within territory and jurisdiction; Art 2(2) legislative/other measures; Art 2(3) effective remedy (HRC General Comment 31); Art 2(1) ICESCR progressive realisation.

cards.q: [Feb 2024 · Q3(c)] The president of Cumri finally declares that Cumri could always and at any time restrict any individual human right in a given case. May a state restrict human rights? Under what conditions? (5 points)
cards.a:
Yes, most rights may be restricted, but only under strict conditions, and some are absolute → "always, any right" is wrong.
• Absolute: torture and ill-treatment (Art 7 ICCPR, Art 3 ECHR), slavery (Art 8(1)–(2) ICCPR), apartheid — never restricted.
• Limitation of qualified rights (e.g. Arts 12(3), 18(3), 19(3), 21, 22(2) ICCPR): (1) provided by law — accessible, precise; (2) legitimate aim — national security, public order, health, morals, rights of others; (3) necessary and proportionate — suitable, least restrictive, fair balance; plus non-discrimination, essence preserved.
• Derogation (Art 4 ICCPR, Art 15 ECHR): public emergency threatening the life of the nation, officially proclaimed; only as strictly required, consistent with other IL duties, non-discriminatory; notified via UN Secretary-General (Art 4(3)).
• Non-derogable (Art 4(2)): Arts 6, 7, 8(1)–(2), 11, 15, 16, 18.
• Each restriction reviewable (HRC, regional courts).

cards.q: Name and explain the circumstances precluding wrongfulness under the ILC Articles on State Responsibility. Which limits apply to all of them? (5 points)
cards.a:
Six circumstances (Arts 20–25 ARSIWA), common limits Arts 26–27.
• Consent (Art 20): valid, before or during the act, within its limits.
• Lawful self-defence (Art 21; Art 51 UN Charter); countermeasures (Art 22; Arts 49–54): non-forcible, against a prior wrong, to induce compliance.
• Force majeure (Art 23): irresistible force or unforeseen event → performance materially impossible; not if self-caused or risk assumed.
• Distress (Art 24): only reasonable way to save own life or lives in one's care; not if self-caused or creating comparable or greater peril.
• Necessity (Art 25): only way to safeguard an essential interest against grave and imminent peril, not seriously impairing others' essential interests; not if the obligation excludes it or self-contributed (Gabčíkovo 1997).
• Limits: never against ius cogens (Art 26); obligation revives once circumstance ceases, compensation for material loss (Art 27).

cards.q: State R unlawfully seizes a merchant ship flying the flag of State S and still holds it after three months; the cargo is damaged, the owner loses a lucrative follow-up contract, and R's minister publicly insults S. What can S claim from R? (4 points)
cards.a:
S can claim cessation, non-repetition and full reparation.
• Cessation of the continuing act → release the ship; assurances and guarantees of non-repetition if circumstances require (Art 30 ARSIWA).
• Full reparation wiping out all consequences (Art 31; Chorzów Factory 1928), forms in fixed order (Art 34): restitution (Art 35) → return ship and cargo unless materially impossible or disproportionate.
• Compensation (Art 36): damaged cargo (damnum emergens), lost contract (lucrum cessans, if established) plus interest (Art 38).
• Satisfaction (Art 37): for the insult → acknowledgment, regret, formal apology; not disproportionate or humiliating.
• As flag state S claims for ship, cargo and crew as a unit (M/V Saiga No. 2, ITLOS 1999).

cards.q: State X expropriates without compensation all assets of nationals of State Y. Y responds by (1) freezing the assets of X's state-owned trading company in Y, (2) suspending a bilateral trade treaty with X, (3) expelling X's ambassador, (4) searching X's embassy and seizing its archives, (5) threatening a naval blockade of X's ports, and (6) suspending fair-trial guarantees for X's nationals in Y. Which measures are lawful? (5 points)
cards.a:
(1), (2) possible countermeasures, (3) lawful retorsion; (4)–(6) prohibited.
• Countermeasures (Arts 22, 49–54 ARSIWA): prior wrongful act of X (uncompensated expropriation → yes); only against X, not third states, to induce compliance, temporary and reversible (Art 49); call to comply, notification, offer to negotiate (Art 52(1)); proportionate (Art 51; Gabčíkovo 1997).

• (3) Expelling the ambassador → retorsion: unfriendly but lawful (persona non grata, Art 9 VCDR).
• (4) Embassy search, archives → diplomatic inviolability (Art 50(2)(b) ARSIWA; Arts 22, 24 VCDR) → prohibited.
• (5) Blockade threat → threat of force (Art 50(1)(a); Art 2(4) UN Charter); (6) fair trial → fundamental human rights (Art 50(1)(b)) → both prohibited.

cards.q: Explain the right of peoples to self-determination: its legal sources, its holder, the difference between internal and external self-determination, and its legal quality (erga omnes, ius cogens). (4 points)
cards.a:
Collective right of peoples freely to determine their political status and development; erga omnes, widely seen as ius cogens.
• Sources: Arts 1(2), 55 UN Charter; common Art 1 ICCPR/ICESCR; GA Res 1514 (1960), Friendly Relations Declaration 1970; custom (Chagos AO 2019).
• Holder: a people → objective features (ethnicity, language, culture, history) + subjective will, or territorial unit (colonial population, uti possidetis).
• Internal: free choice of political, economic, social, cultural system within the existing state.
• External: independence, free association or integration (Res 1541) → colonial, occupied or alien-dominated peoples; remedial secession only argued.
• Quality: erga omnes (East Timor 1995; Wall 2004; Chagos 2019); ius cogens (ILC Draft Conclusions 2022).

cards.q: In 1948 the UN mediator Count Folke Bernadotte was murdered in Jerusalem. The UN Charter contains no provision allowing the UN to bring international claims. What did the ICJ hold in the Reparation for Injuries advisory opinion (1949), and why is it fundamental for the law of international organizations? Could the UN claim even against a state that was not a UN member at the time? (4 points)
cards.a:
The UN has international legal personality and may claim for injury to itself and to its agent, even against non-member Israel.
• Personality inferred from the functions and rights the Charter gives the UN (organs, tasks, treaty-making, privileges); subject of IL, not a state.
• Implied powers: powers conferred by necessary implication as essential to performing its duties → claims for own damage and functional protection of its agent (coordinate with national state, no double recovery).
• Objective personality: 50 states, the vast majority of the community, created it → valid also against non-members.
• Significance: basis of implied powers and functional IO personality (Effects of Awards 1954, Certain Expenses 1962).

cards.q: Which types of organs do international organizations typically have? Name the forms of decision-making used in international organizations and the exceptions to the principle "one state, one vote", with an example of each. (3 points)
cards.a:
Plenary organ, council and secretariat (often also parliamentary, expert, judicial bodies); unanimity, majority or consensus; departures: veto and weighted voting.
• Organs: plenary (UN General Assembly), council of limited membership (Security Council), secretariat (Secretary-General); parliaments (European Parliament), experts (ILC), courts (ICJ).

• Departures: P5 veto (Art 27(3) UN Charter); weighting by capital (IMF, World Bank) or population (EU Council QMV, Art 16(4) TEU).

cards.q: States Pora and Quin conclude a canal treaty. It grants all merchant ships of State Rin free passage and obliges State Sella, an upstream neighbour, to keep the water level constant. Rin's ships use the canal; Sella never reacts. Later Pora and Quin wish to abolish Rin's right of passage. What is the legal position of Rin and Sella? (3 points)

Rin has the right; Sella is not bound; Rin's right is revocable unless intended to be irrevocable.
• Pacta tertiis: no rights or obligations for third states without consent (Art 34 VCLT).
• Rights (Art 36(1)): parties' intent + assent, presumed unless contrary indicated → Rin's use confirms it.
• Obligations (Art 35): parties' intent + express written acceptance → Sella's silence insufficient.
• Revocation (Art 37(2)): impossible if intended not revocable without Rin's consent; otherwise Pora and Quin may abolish it.

cards.q: Soldiers of State N (not a party to the Rome Statute), on the orders of N's President, kill hundreds of civilians on the territory of State P (a party) during an armed conflict. cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? 'A soldier who follows orders cannot be punished, and his commander is liable only if he personally ordered the crimes.' Give reasons. (2 points)
cards.a:
No — superior orders are generally no defence; commanders are also liable for omissions.
• Superior orders (Nuremberg Principle IV; Art 33 Rome Statute): excuse only if legal duty to obey, unaware of unlawfulness and not manifestly unlawful; genocide/CAH orders always manifestly unlawful.

cards.q: Name and briefly explain the sources of international law listed in Article 38(1) of the ICJ Statute. Which sources are not listed there, and what is the status of judicial decisions and teachings? (5 points)
cards.a:
Art 38(1) ICJ Statute: (a)–(c) are the formal sources, (d) only subsidiary means; binding IO decisions and unilateral acts are sources not listed.
• (a) Treaties: express consent → bind only the parties (Art 34 VCLT).
• (b) Custom: general state practice + opinio iuris → binds all states except persistent objectors.
• (c) General principles of law recognised by civilized nations (good faith, estoppel, res judicata) → fill gaps, no non liquet.
• (d) Judicial decisions and teachings of the most highly qualified publicists = subsidiary means, subject to Art 59 (binding only between the parties, no stare decisis) → do not create law.
• Not listed: SC Chapter VII resolutions (Art 25 UN Charter), unilateral acts (Nuclear Tests 1974); soft law (UDHR, GA resolutions) is no source.
• No hierarchy among the sources; only ius cogens ranks higher.

cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? Give reasons. "Because treaties are listed first in Article 38(1) of the ICJ Statute, a treaty always prevails over a conflicting rule of customary international law." (3 points)
cards.a:
No — treaties and custom are of equal rank; Art 38(1) is a list, not a hierarchy.
• Conflicts are resolved by lex specialis (the more specific rule prevails) and lex posterior (the later rule prevails, cf. Art 30(3) VCLT); later custom can modify a treaty.
• → A treaty prevails only where it is the special or the later rule.
• Only real hierarchy: ius cogens voids conflicting treaties (Arts 53, 64 VCLT); Art 103 UN Charter gives Charter obligations priority over other treaties.

cards.q: Distinguish obligations erga omnes from ius cogens. State Tarsia commits genocide against a minority on its own territory. May State Uldonia, none of whose nationals are affected, invoke Tarsia's international responsibility? (3 points)
cards.a:
Yes — the genocide prohibition is ius cogens and erga omnes → any state may invoke it.
• Ius cogens = rank: non-derogable, conflicting treaty void (Art 53 VCLT).
• Erga omnes = owed to the whole international community → every state has a legal interest (Barcelona Traction 1970); all ius cogens is erga omnes, not vice versa.
• Uldonia, not injured (Art 42 ARSIWA), invokes Art 48(1)(b) ARSIWA → cessation, non-repetition, reparation for victims (Art 48(2)); if a party, ICJ under Art IX Genocide Convention (The Gambia v Myanmar).

cards.topic: General Principles of Law, Unilateral Acts and Subsidiary Means
cards.q: State Lumeria conducted atmospheric nuclear tests. After worldwide protests, its President declares at a televised press conference, and its Foreign Minister repeats before the UN General Assembly, that "Lumeria will conduct no further atmospheric tests". A year later a new government announces new tests, arguing that press statements are political and non-binding because no treaty was concluded. Is Lumeria bound? Explain the concept and the conditions of binding unilateral declarations. (4 points)
cards.a:
Yes — a public, clear declaration by a competent organ intending to be bound binds through good faith, no treaty needed (Nuclear Tests 1974).
• Unilateral act: source outside Art 38 ICJ Statute; no quid pro quo or acceptance, form irrelevant.
• Conditions (ILC Guiding Principles 2006): competent organ: head of state/government, foreign minister (GP 4; Eastern Greenland 1933); public; clear and specific terms, interpreted restrictively (GP 7); intention to be bound; not contrary to ius cogens (GP 8).
• Application: President and Foreign Minister, repeated, specific, after protests → intention to be bound.
• New government irrelevant (continuity); no arbitrary revocation (GP 10) → new tests unlawful.
• Contrast: Burkina Faso/Mali 1986 (no intent).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Name and explain the criteria of statehood under international law. Which criterion is disputed, and what happens to an existing state that loses its effective government? (4 points)
cards.a:
Statehood: permanent population, defined territory, effective and independent government (Art 1 Montevideo Convention 1933); capacity for relations is disputed; an existing state survives loss of government.
• Population: stable, linked by nationality; no minimum size (Nauru).
• Territory: stable core suffices; border disputes no obstacle (North Sea Continental Shelf 1969).
• Government: effective control + independence, formal (Austro-German Customs Union, PCIJ 1931) and actual (no puppet: Manchukuo 1932).
• Capacity for relations (Art 1(d)): disputed → consequence of independence, not a separate criterion.
• Loss of government: strict test for new, lenient for existing states → presumption of continuity (Somalia after 1991).
• Created in breach of ius cogens → no state (Southern Rhodesia, TRNC).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? 'An entity becomes a state only when it has been recognised by other states.' Give reasons. (3 points)
cards.a:
No — under the prevailing declaratory theory statehood follows from the factual criteria (population, territory, effective government); recognition only confirms it.
• Declaratory: Art 3 Montevideo Convention (political existence independent of recognition); Badinter Commission Opinion No 1 (1991): statehood is a question of fact.
• Constitutive theory (recognition creates the state) rejected: relativity, no central organ, unrecognised entities are still bound and protected (prohibition of force).
• Recognition still matters: evidence in doubtful cases (Kosovo), diplomatic relations and treaties, effects before domestic courts.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Ms K, a national of State A working in State B, uses her laptop in B to hack the power grid of State C, causing a blackout there, steals credit-card data of nationals of State D and prints counterfeit banknotes of State E. She then travels to State F, which has no link to the facts. Which states may exercise criminal jurisdiction, and on what basis? May C send police officers to F to arrest her there? (5 points)
cards.a:
A, B, C, D and E each have a sufficient link to prescribe and adjudicate; F has none (no universal crime); C may not arrest K in F without F's consent → extradition request.
• B: territoriality – acts committed there.
• C: objective territoriality/effects – blackout there (Lotus 1927) + protective principle (critical infrastructure).
• A: active personality – K is its national; D: passive personality – victims are its nationals.
• E: protective principle – counterfeiting of its currency threatens vital interests.
• F: universality only for piracy, genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, torture → not here; at most vicarious jurisdiction or a treaty duty (Art 9 1929 Counterfeiting Convention).
• Enforcement jurisdiction strictly territorial (Lotus 1927) → arrest by C's police in F violates F's sovereignty (Eichmann 1960) → C must request extradition.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: What is the legal basis of state immunity? Explain the difference between absolute and restrictive immunity and how acta iure imperii are distinguished from acta iure gestionis. (4 points)
cards.a:
Immunity rests on sovereign equality (par in parem non habet imperium); absolute immunity covered all acts, restrictive immunity only acta iure imperii, distinguished primarily by nature.
• Basis: Art 2(1) UN Charter; custom (Jurisdictional Immunities, ICJ 2012); ECSI 1972; UNCSI 2004 (not in force, reflects custom).
• Absolute: a foreign state can never be sued domestically; restrictive: acta iure gestionis not immune (Dralle, OGH 1950).
• Nature: could a private person do it? Sale, lease, loan = gestionis; legislation, police, military, expropriation = imperii; purpose only secondarily (Art 2(2) UNCSI; Empire of Iran, BVerfG 1963).
• Exceptions (UNCSI): commercial transactions (Art 10), employment (Art 11), torts in the forum (Art 12); consent (Arts 7–8).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: The embassy of State F in Vienna orders a heating system from the Austrian company Wärme GmbH and does not pay. Wärme sues F before the Austrian courts, wins, and seeks enforcement against (1) the embassy's bank account used for salaries and rent, (2) a building owned by F in Vienna rented out as offices to private companies, (3) reserves of F's central bank deposited in Austria. Assess immunity from jurisdiction and from enforcement. (4 points)
cards.a:
No immunity from jurisdiction (commercial act); enforcement only against the commercially rented building.
• Jurisdiction: restrictive immunity, nature of the act decides → contract for work = actum iure gestionis (Empire of Iran, BVerfG 1963; Art 10 UNCSI).
• Enforcement separate: purpose of the asset when execution begins → sovereign-purpose property immune without consent (Philippine Embassy, BVerfG 1977; Art 19 UNCSI).
• (1) Embassy account serves the mission → immune, even if mixed (Art 21(1)(a) UNCSI; Art 25 VCDR).
• (2) Building rented out commercially → non-governmental purpose → seizable (Art 19(c) UNCSI).
• (3) Central bank reserves → immune (Art 21(1)(c) UNCSI).
• Waiver of jurisdiction ≠ waiver of enforcement (Art 20 UNCSI).

cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? 'A state is responsible under international law only if it acted with fault and caused material damage.' Give reasons. (3 points)
cards.a:
No — every internationally wrongful act entails responsibility (Art 1 ARSIWA): conduct attributable to the state that breaches an international obligation (Art 2); fault and damage are not general elements.
• Fault: objective responsibility; required only where the primary rule says so (knowledge/due diligence – Corfu Channel 1949; genocidal intent).
• Damage: the breach itself is the legal injury (Rainbow Warrior 1990); damage matters only for reparation (Art 31(2)) and the injured state (Art 42).
• Wrongfulness is excluded only by circumstances under Arts 20–25 ARSIWA.
